1000018.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Finnland, from finnar (“Sami; Finns”) + land (“land, country”), literally “land of the Finns”. The name originally referred to the southwestern region now known as Egentliga Finland, before being extended to the whole country.
Compare Swedish Finland, Faroese Finnland, Icelandic Finnland and the parallel Old English Finna land (“Lapland; land of the Sami”).
The first element is commonly traced to *finnaz (“Sami; Finn”), of disputed origin; compare Old English Finn (“Sami”). The second element continues *landą (“land, country”) and is cognate with English land, Dutch la

1001554.etyen:
Derived from Old Norse Magna (“female given name”), either by continuation or revival. The Old Norse name is the feminine form of Magni (“male given name”), from magn (“might, strength”). The modern Norwegian name may also be a short form of compound names containing this element, especially Magnhild, or a feminine derivative of Magnus, ultimately from Latin magnus (“great”). First attested in 1310 in Norway; documented again in modern use from 1850.
Compare Danish Magna, Swedish Magna, Icelandic Magna and Faroese Magna (“female given name”).
